toc.title: Impediments and the Scrum Master's Accountability (CSM 3.6)
How the Scrum Master Assists the Team with Impediments (CSM 3.6)

Why Scrum Has No Project Manager (CSM 3.9)
Exam Traps and What the Exam Expects

html:
1Impediments and the Scrum Master's Accountability (CSM 3.6)

An impediment is anything that blocks or slows the Scrum Team's progress toward its goals. The Guide uses the word without defining it.

What the Guide says Meaning
The Scrum Master serves the team by "causing the removal of impediments to the Scrum Team's progress" The Scrum Master is accountable for the result: the impediment goes away. The team, the Scrum Master or others in the organization may do the work
The Scrum Master serves the organization by "removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams" Some impediments sit in the organization and need the Scrum Master to work with managers and stakeholders
Adaptation must happen "as soon as possible to minimize further deviation" Impediments are raised and acted on early, not saved for later
The Daily Scrum "identifies impediments" The team surfaces them every working day

1.1 Two levels of impediment

Level Examples Who resolves
Team level A broken build, an unclear item, a missing skill, a conflict in the team The team, with the Scrum Master's coaching and facilitation
Organizational level Members assigned to several projects, slow approvals, no test environment, managers overruling the Product Owner The Scrum Master, working with managers and other groups, supported by the team

2Organizational Impediments (CSM 3.5)

The objective asks for at least three Beyond the Guide.

Organizational impediment Why it blocks the Scrum Team
Members split across several projects or teams The team is not able to focus or be cross-functional; the Sprint Goal competes with other work
Functional silos and hand-offs (separate test, operations, database or design groups) The team depends on others to finish an Increment, so work waits and quality suffers
Slow approval chains and phase gates Decisions take longer than the Sprint; adaptation is delayed
Managers or stakeholders overruling the Product Owner, or no empowered Product Owner The Product Backlog loses its order; the Guide says the whole organization must respect the Product Owner's decisions
Command-and-control management A team told how and who is not self-managing and cannot adapt "the moment it learns anything new"
Stakeholders not available for Product Backlog refinement or the Sprint Review Feedback is late; the Product Owner works blind
Traditional metrics and incentives (individual utilization, fixed scope and date) They reward the wrong behaviour: working to the plan, not delivering value
Fixed-scope contracts and annual project budgets They resist the change that empiricism expects
Missing tools, environments or access The team cannot complete work that meets its Definition of Done
Policies that mandate events or documents that do not fit They add work that does not serve the product
Skipping or shortening Scrum events under pressure Opportunities to inspect and adapt are lost (Topic 6)

3How the Scrum Master Assists the Team with Impediments (CSM 3.6)

The objective asks for at least two ways Beyond the Guide, built on the Guide's duties:

Way What it looks like
Make impediments visible Raise them at the Daily Scrum, keep an impediment list or board, show their cost in lost time
Coach the team to resolve what it can Ask questions so that the team solves team-level problems itself (self-management)
Remove what the team cannot Work with managers, other teams or stakeholders on organizational impediments
Find the root cause Help the team look beyond symptoms (see section 4)
Escalate with evidence Bring data (time lost, quality effects) to the people who can act
Facilitate resolution sessions Bring the right people together and keep the conversation neutral and productive
Follow through and learn Check that the impediment is gone; use the Retrospective to prevent its return
Protect the team's focus Help the organization understand how its actions affect the team (Topic 5)
Exam angle

the best answer to a blocked team is usually make it visible, find the right people, and get it removed, not "fix it alone", "tell the team to cope" or "wait until the Retrospective". For an organizational impediment the Scrum Master works with the organization.

4Techniques to Resolve an Impediment (CSM 3.7)Beyond the Guide

The objective asks you to apply at least one. Common ones:

Technique How it works Good for
5 Whys Ask "why?" repeatedly (about five times) until the root cause shows One problem with a chain of causes
Fishbone (cause and effect) diagram Group possible causes by category (people, process, tools, environment, policy) around the problem A problem with many possible causes
Impediment board or list, prioritized Make every impediment visible, rank by impact and urgency, start with the most harmful or easiest Many impediments at once
Escalation with data Bring evidence (days lost, defects) to the decision maker who can act Organizational impediments
Facilitated working session Bring the affected people together to design a solution Impediments that need agreement between groups
Small experiment Try a limited change, check the result in the next Sprint, keep or drop it Unclear solutions; supports empiricism
Retrospective problem-solving Choose the most impactful impediment and plan its removal Recurring problems

4.1 Worked example: the 5 Whys

Problem: the Increment is not ready to demonstrate at the Sprint Review.

  1. Why was it not ready? Testing was not finished.
  2. Why was testing not finished? The test environment was down for three days.
  3. Why was it down? The environment is shared with another project that was using it.
  4. Why was it used by two projects? Nobody owns the scheduling of the shared environment.
  5. Why does nobody own it? The organization never assigned an owner.

Root cause: no owner for the shared environment. Action: the Scrum Master works with management to assign an owner or give the team its own environment, and the team raises the cost (three days lost) as evidence.

5Technical Debt (CSM 3.2)Beyond the Guide

The Guide does not mention technical debt. In common usage it is the implied cost of future rework caused by choosing an easy or limited solution now instead of a better approach that would take longer. Like financial debt, it carries "interest": the longer it stays, the more it costs.

5.1 Impact of accumulating technical debt

Impact Explanation
Slower delivery over time Every change takes longer because the code or design is hard to change
Higher cost of change and maintenance Rework and workarounds consume effort that could create value
More defects and incidents Fragile parts break, bugs appear, customers are affected
Reduced predictability Estimates and forecasts are less reliable; surprises grow
Less ability to respond to change The product is harder to adapt, which undermines agility
Lower morale Teams working in a poor code base become frustrated
Risk to quality and the Increment The Increment may stop being usable or truly "Done"

5.2 How Scrum deals with it

  • The Definition of Done is the first defence: work that does not meet the quality measures is not Done (Topic 12). "Quality does not decrease" during the Sprint.
  • Transparency: make the debt visible, for example as Product Backlog items, so that the Product Owner can weigh it against new features.
  • The Developers plan the work needed to meet the Definition of Done and are accountable for quality; the Product Owner orders the Product Backlog, including debt work; the Scrum Master helps everyone see the impact.
  • Practitioners warn against separate "debt" or "hardening" Sprints: Scrum puts all necessary work inside every Sprint (Topic 6).

6Development Practices That Raise Quality and Reduce Debt (CSM 3.3)Beyond the Guide

The objective asks for at least three. These practices come from extreme programming and DevOps and are widely taught with Scrum. The Developers choose which to use; the Scrum Master encourages them and helps remove the barriers to them.

Practice What it is How it helps
Test-driven development (TDD) Write a failing automated test first, then the code that passes it Clean, testable design; immediate feedback
Automated testing (unit, integration, regression) Tests run by tools, not by hand Fast, repeatable checks; confidence to change code
Continuous integration Developers integrate their work frequently and an automated build and test runs each time Integration problems appear early; the product always works together
Continuous delivery and deployment automation Automated build, test and release steps Reliable, frequent, low-risk delivery of usable Increments
Refactoring Improving the structure of code without changing its behaviour Removes debt before it grows
Pair and mob programming Two or more people work on the same code together Shared knowledge, fewer defects, instant review
Code reviews and coding standards Peers check the work against agreed standards Consistency and early defect discovery
Simple design Build what is needed now and keep the design clear Less to maintain
A strong Definition of Done Includes tests, reviews, security and integration Makes quality a condition for every item

7Organizational Design Changes Caused by Adopting Scrum (CSM 3.8)Beyond the Guide

The objective asks you to summarize at least one. Scrum does not leave an organization's structure untouched:

From To
Functional departments and component teams Cross-functional product teams that hold all skills needed to create an Increment
Temporary project teams Stable teams around a product, working toward a Product Goal
A manager or project manager assigning work Self-managing teams that decide who does what, when and how
Managers as controllers Managers as leaders, coaches and enablers who build the environment for the team
Hand-off between analysis, design, build and test One team doing all of it each Sprint
Quality assurance as a department at the end Quality built in through the Definition of Done
Requirements documents passed to the team A Product Owner and an ordered Product Backlog that stay in conversation with the team
Funding fixed-scope projects Funding products and Product Goals, and judging progress by delivered value
Many management layers Fewer layers, with decisions closer to the work

The most affected people are usually managers and project managers, whose roles change from directing to enabling (see section 8).

8Why Scrum Has No Project Manager (CSM 3.9)Beyond the Guide

The Guide defines three accountabilities (Developers, Product Owner, Scrum Master) and states that within a Scrum Team there are no sub-teams or hierarchies. It has no project manager role. The reasons:

Reason Explanation
Self-management The team decides who does what, when and how. A person who assigns and controls work would remove that
No hierarchy The Scrum Team is one cohesive unit; a project manager would create a level above the others
Empiricism, not detailed up-front control Scrum inspects and adapts every Sprint instead of managing a detailed plan against a baseline
The duties are shared among the three accountabilities The work a project manager does is still done, but by the people closest to it
One goal at a time The Product Goal, one Product Backlog and one Product Owner give direction without a project manager

Traditional project management duty Where it lives in Scrum
Define scope and priorities The Product Owner, through the Product Backlog and the Product Goal
Plan and estimate the work The Developers, through Sprint Planning, the Sprint Backlog and sizing
Assign tasks Nobody: the Developers decide who does what
Manage quality The Developers, through the Definition of Done
Communicate with stakeholders The Product Owner and the Scrum Team, mainly at the Sprint Review; the Scrum Master facilitates as needed
Manage risks and changes Built into the empirical loop: each Sprint inspects and adapts; the Product Owner reorders the Product Backlog
Remove blockers and keep the process working The Scrum Master
Report status Transparency of the artifacts and the Increment, not reports

Scrum does not reject project management skills. People who were project managers can serve as Product Owner, Scrum Master or Developer, or serve the organization in other roles. What does not exist is a role above the Scrum Team that directs it.

9Exam Traps and What the Exam Expects

  1. The Scrum Master is accountable for causing the removal of impediments (not for personally fixing every one, and not for waiting).
  2. Visible first. Impediments are raised at the Daily Scrum and made visible; waiting for the Retrospective is slow.
  3. Organizational impediments need work with the organization. Coaching the team to "cope" does not remove them.
  4. Root cause beats symptom. Techniques such as 5 Whys and fishbone find causes.
  5. The Definition of Done is the main defence against technical debt. Lowering it increases debt.
  6. Technical debt is not in the Guide. If a question uses it, answer from the impact: slower delivery, higher cost, more defects.
  7. No hardening, release or debt Sprints. All necessary work happens inside every Sprint.
  8. Practices are the Developers' choice; the Scrum Master encourages, the Product Owner orders debt work with the rest.
  9. There is no project manager in Scrum. Duties are shared; nobody assigns tasks or sits above the team.
  10. Organizational design changes: cross-functional product teams, self-managing teams, managers as enablers, quality built in.
  11. A change in the organization needs leadership. The Scrum Master leads, trains and coaches the organization in its Scrum adoption.

10Exam Q&A

10.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1The team's members are each assigned to two other projects by their functional managers, and the Sprint Goals keep slipping. What is the best action for the Scrum Master?

  • AWork with the managers to make the impact visible and help dedicate the people to the Scrum Team
  • BTell the Developers to work faster
  • CReduce the Definition of Done
  • DWait for the Retrospective
Show the answer

Answer: A. Members split across projects are an organizational impediment. The Scrum Master is accountable for causing the removal of impediments and serves the organization by working on barriers with managers. Pressing the team or lowering quality does not remove the cause.

S2The Increment was late again. The Scrum Master asks "why?" five times and traces it to a shared test environment that nobody owns. Which technique is this?

  • AThe 5 Whys
  • BA dot vote
  • CA fishbone diagram
  • DA burn-down chart
Show the answer

Answer: A. Repeatedly asking why to reach the root cause is the 5 Whys technique. A fishbone groups possible causes, dot voting selects among options and a burn-down shows progress.

S3An impediment needs a decision from a senior executive whom the Scrum Master cannot reach directly. What should the Scrum Master do?

  • AAsk the Developers to solve it themselves, because the impediment needs a decision that only they can take
  • BMake the impediment visible with evidence of its cost and work with those who can reach the executive
  • CIgnore it until the next Sprint, as the executive may decide differently once the quarter has ended
  • DCancel the Sprint and ask the Product Owner to plan a new one without the blocked work
Show the answer

Answer: B. The Scrum Master is accountable for causing the removal of impediments and serves the organization by removing barriers. Bringing evidence to those who can act is how an organizational impediment is escalated. Cancelling a Sprint is for an obsolete Sprint Goal only.

S4The Product Owner wants only new features, while the code base is getting harder to change and defects are rising. What is the best way for the Scrum Master to help?

  • AAgree and ask the team to hurry, because new features create the value that the stakeholders are waiting for in the next release
  • BPlan a hardening Sprint after the next release, in which the Developers fix the defects and clean the code
  • CAsk the Developers to work overtime to clear the defects, while they continue to deliver the new features
  • DMake the debt and its impact visible so the Product Owner can weigh it, and keep quality in the Definition of Done
Show the answer

Answer: D. Technical debt slows delivery and raises cost and risk over time. Making it visible lets the Product Owner order debt work with the other items, and the Definition of Done keeps quality from decreasing. A separate hardening Sprint is not part of Scrum.

S5Which set of practices would help a team deliver high-quality Increments and reduce technical debt?

  • ALonger Sprints, fewer meetings, more documentation
  • BAutomated testing, continuous integration and refactoring
  • CHiring more managers
  • DLarger Product Backlog items
Show the answer

Answer: B. Automated testing, continuous integration and refactoring give fast feedback and keep the code base clean, which keeps Increments usable and debt low. The other options do not address quality directly.

S6A manager asks who the project manager is in a Scrum Team. What is the best answer?

  • AThe Scrum Master, who coordinates the team, assigns the tasks and is accountable for the delivery of the Sprint
  • BThe Product Owner, who is accountable for the product and decides what is built in every Sprint
  • CScrum has no project manager: the three accountabilities share the duties and the Scrum Team is self-managing
  • DThe most senior Developer, who plans the work and assigns the tasks to the other Developers in the team
Show the answer

Answer: C. Scrum defines three accountabilities and no hierarchy. Scope and priorities sit with the Product Owner, planning and quality with the Developers, and the process and impediments with the Scrum Master.

S7After adopting Scrum, a company merges its separate analysis, development and test departments into cross-functional product teams. How is this described?

  • AAn organizational design change caused by adopting Scrum
  • BA violation of Scrum
  • CA temporary phase
  • DAn example of a hardening Sprint
Show the answer

Answer: A. Moving from functional departments to cross-functional teams that contain all the skills for an Increment is a typical organizational design change that follows from Scrum.

S8Which of the following is an organizational impediment?

  • AA Developer is on holiday for two weeks, so the team has less capacity than the Sprint Backlog was planned for
  • BA build failed for an hour, because a Developer checked in a change that broke the automated tests
  • CA Developer needs to learn a tool that the team has chosen, which takes a few days of pairing with a colleague
  • DManagement requires every change to pass a three-week approval board before the team can release
Show the answer

Answer: D. A slow approval chain imposed by the organization limits the whole Scrum Team and cannot be fixed by the team alone. The other options are normal team-level matters.

S9Which description of technical debt is best?

  • AA financial loan that the team takes from the organization to buy tools and then repays over several Sprints, with interest
  • BA list of unfinished Product Backlog items that the team carries from one Sprint to the next Sprint
  • CThe implied cost of future rework caused by choosing an easy or limited solution now over a better approach
  • DA debt owed to stakeholders when the team does not deliver everything that was promised in the Sprint
Show the answer

Answer: C. The term describes the later cost of shortcuts in the product's code or design. It is a metaphor, not money borrowed.

S10A team member says: "We cannot do anything until the Scrum Master removes this impediment." What is the best correction?

  • AThe Scrum Master alone must remove every impediment, so the team should wait and not start any other work until the Scrum Master has reported back
  • BThe Scrum Master is accountable for getting it removed; the team removes what it can while the Scrum Master works on the rest
  • CImpediments are not the Scrum Master's job, because the team is self-managing and solves every problem itself
  • DThe Product Owner must remove it, since the Product Owner is accountable for the value that the team delivers
Show the answer

Answer: B. The Scrum Master causes the removal of impediments to the team's progress; the team and others may do the work. The team coached toward self-management solves team-level problems itself.

10.2 Recall Q&As

R1What does the Guide say about impediments?

Show the answer

The Scrum Master serves the team by causing the removal of impediments to its progress, and serves the organization by removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams.

R2Name three organizational impediments.

Show the answer

Members split across projects; functional silos and hand-offs; slow approvals; managers overruling the Product Owner; command-and-control management; unavailable stakeholders; traditional metrics; missing tools or environments.

R3Name two ways the Scrum Master assists the team with impediments.

Show the answer

Make them visible; coach the team to resolve what it can; remove what it cannot with the organization; find the root cause; escalate with evidence; follow through.

R4Name two techniques for resolving an impediment.

Show the answer

5 Whys; fishbone diagram; a prioritized impediment board; escalation with data; a facilitated working session; a small experiment.

R5What is technical debt?

Show the answer

The implied cost of future rework caused by choosing an easy or limited solution now instead of a better approach.

R6Name three impacts of technical debt.

Show the answer

Slower delivery; higher cost of change; more defects; less predictability; less ability to adapt; lower morale.

R7What is the Scrum team's main defence against technical debt?

Show the answer

The Definition of Done, plus transparency of the debt and engineering practices.

R8Name three practices that raise quality and reduce debt.

Show the answer

Test-driven development; automated testing; continuous integration; continuous delivery; refactoring; pair or mob programming; code reviews.

R9Does Scrum use a hardening Sprint for debt?

Show the answer

No. All necessary work is done within every Sprint; quality is built in.

R10Name one organizational design change caused by adopting Scrum.

Show the answer

Functional departments become cross-functional product teams; managers become enablers; teams become self-managing; quality is built in; products are funded instead of projects.

R11How many accountabilities does Scrum define?

Show the answer

Three: the Developers, the Product Owner and the Scrum Master.

R12Why does Scrum have no project manager?

Show the answer

The team is self-managing with no hierarchy, Scrum uses empiricism rather than detailed up-front control, and the duties are shared among the three accountabilities.

R13Where does the Scrum Master's accountability for impediments come from?

Show the answer

The Guide: causing the removal of impediments to the Scrum Team's progress; removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams.

R14Where do project management duties go in Scrum?

Show the answer

Scope and priorities to the Product Owner; planning, estimating and quality to the Developers; process and impediments to the Scrum Master; reporting is replaced by transparency.

11Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Impediment Anything blocking the team's progress; the Scrum Master causes its removal
Levels Team level (team resolves) · organizational level (Scrum Master works with the organization)
Organizational examples Split assignment · silos · slow approvals · overruled Product Owner · command and control · unavailable stakeholders · bad metrics
Scrum Master assists Make visible · coach · remove · root cause · escalate with data · facilitate · follow through
Techniques 5 Whys · fishbone · impediment board · escalation with data · working session · experiment
Technical debt Implied cost of future rework from an easy solution now; not in the Guide
Impact Slower delivery · higher cost · more defects · less predictability · less adaptability · lower morale
Defence Definition of Done · visibility · engineering practices; no hardening Sprint
Practices Test-driven development · automated tests · continuous integration · continuous delivery · refactoring · pair or mob programming · code review
Design changes Cross-functional product teams · self-managing · managers as enablers · quality built in · fund products
No project manager Three accountabilities, no hierarchy; duties shared: Product Owner scope, Developers plan and quality, Scrum Master process
